GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: Chances for light precipitation (valley rain, mountain snow above 10,000 feet) continue through the weekend as a low pressure system, currently spinning off the California coast, traverses the Intermountain West.
GJT.text:
HAZARDOUS WEATHER POSSIBLE THROUGH FRIDAY:

Remnant moisture from a tropical cyclone formerly known as Trudy will move into the Four Corners tomorrow before tracking northeastward across eastern Utah and western Colorado through Friday morning. A plethora of weather hazards are possible with this system including flooding, flash flooding, strong to severe thunderstorms, and snow above 12,000-13,000 feet. As a result, a Flood watch has been issued for parts of southeast Utah and southwest Colorado from 12 PM Wednesday through 12 PM Friday.

Showers and storms develop along the moisture transport gradient as early as tomorrow morning, with storms strengthening throughout the afternoon. This initial push of convection tomorrow will pose a localized threat for heavy rainfall and flash flooding if stronger storms develop, especially if storms begin to train over the same areas. Isolated severe storms are possible in the Four Corners region capable of producing large hail, damaging wind, and brief tornadoes as well due to the presence of modest instability and strong shear. However, the highest potential for severe weather will remain off to our southwest in northwest into central Arizona. Stay weather aware if you have outdoor activities planned! If you experience any of the hazards noted above, please report them to NWS Grand Junction.

With an anomalously moist tropical airmass overhead, widespread rainfall takes hold of the forecast area Wednesday night. Please see the Hydrology Section below for more information concerning the threat for flooding from this period of moderate to widespread rainfall.

Another round of strong to severe storms cannot be ruled out on Thursday afternoon/evening with marginal instability and strong wind shear present. However, widespread cloud cover adds a layer of uncertainty to the forecast and may inhibit surface heating. BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: A cold front will push through the area Saturday morning, bringing another period of northerly breezy winds with gusts up to 25-30 mph. There is still some model disagreement regarding the strength, and the moisture accompanying this front.
BOU.text:
Recent radar imagery shows a couple of showers moving off the northern CO foothills. These showers are being supported by enhanced vorticity and lift from the weak shortwave moving across northern CO this afternoon. Temperatures are sitting in the 60s to 70s over the Denver metro and plains, with 50s and low 60s across the mountains. Isolated showers will continue to be possible over the high terrain through sunset, although very minimal rainfall (perhaps just a few hundredths) is expected to reach the ground. Skies will be mostly clear tonight with morning lows expected to be slightly warmer than this morning over the plains, with temperatures in the low 50s for the Denver metro, and some mid 40s in the usual cold spots out in the northeast CO plains.

An upper level ridge will begin to build over the area tonight, reinforcing above-average temperatures for the rest of the work week as temperatures soar into the mid to upper 70s at low elevations. This upper level ridge will also strengthen southwest flow aloft and bring an increase in Pacific moisture later in the day ahead of a strong cutoff low to the west. However, we do not expect any rain chances to arrive to the mountains of our area until the late afternoon/early evening. Moisture transport will intensify late Wednesday night as the cutoff low reaches the California coast, and a robust subtropical jet channels Pacific moisture towards the Four Corners in an atmospheric river-like fashion. A first round of isolated showers will be possible into the overnight hours over the mountains, and mid level clouds will begin to drift over the plains.

Shower coverage should increase over the high terrain Thursday afternoon. However, as has been outlined in previous AFDs, southwesterly flow aloft and limited instability will favor more modest rainfall amounts for southwest CO, with much lighter amounts over our CWA. PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: While models continue to indicate run to run differences, however latest data supports the main system lifting north and east across the Northern Rockies on Friday, with secondary energy hanging back across the Four Corners region.
PUB.text:
Model continues to be in good agreement through the end of the work week, with transitory upper ridging building across eastern Colorado through Thursday, as southwest flow increases across western Colorado ahead of an eastern Pacific storm system digging into the Great Basin. Model data supports abundant sup-tropical moisture becoming entrained within the southwest flow aloft, with PWATS of 0.8 to over 1 inch (200-300 percent of normal) moving across the region through Thursday. This, along with increasing orographic flow, and uvv associated with the Pacific system moving across the Great Basin, will lead to increasing coverage and intensity of precipitation along and west of the Continental Divide Wednesday night, with the heaviest precipitation expected Thursday into Thursday night, as the main system starts to lift out across the Great Basin into the Northern Rockies.

Latest model data continues to support qpf of 1 to 3 inches along and west of the ContDvd through this period, with the greatest amounts expected across the San Juan Mtns, where locally up to 4 inches of liquid precipitation will be possible. The Pacific origin of the system is expected to keep snow levels around peak level (at and above 12,000 feet) through the duration of the heavy precipitation event (at least through Thursday night), leading to concerns of river and stream flooding as well as the potential for rock/mudslides across the higher terrain of the ContDvd. The area of greatest concern remains across the San Juan Mtns, with already saturated soils from previous precipitation last week, as well the potential for heavy rain on top of snowpack already in place, with SNOTEL data indicating SWE 3/4 to 1" across the San Juans at this time. CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Tuesday...Day seven shows the typical model discrepancies in this progressive synoptic pattern, leading to a fairly low to moderate confidence forecast.
CYS.text:
Thursday...The beginning of an unsettled and wetter pattern will commence as the initial negatively tilted shortwave trough aloft, emanating from the parent upper trough over southern Nevada, moves northeast across our counties during the daylight hours. Dynamics associated with this perturbation aloft and orographic effects will produce scattered showers in the afternoon across Carbon County, including our Snowy and Sierra Madre Ranges. A lull in shower coverage is expected Thursday night as the southeast Wyoming is somewhat dry slotted. Brisk southerly low level winds will persist Thursday night, along with cloud cover to keep minimum temperatures rather mild.

Friday...The parent shortwave trough aloft, negatively tilted, moves from northern Utah near dawn, to northeast Wyoming by suppertime, with the majority of our forecast locations being dry slotted, as the bulk of the shortwave trough moisture and lift will be over western Wyoming and central Montana. Although, with the approach of the Pacific origin cold front and frontal lifting, as well as some mid level moisture, you can anticipate, scattered afternoon showers for areas bounded roughly by Laramie, Wheatland, Torrington and Cheyenne, with the showers moving and/or developing into far eastern Wyoming and the Nebraska Panhandle in the evening, before showers mainly dissipate late as the rather potent Pacific origin cold front sweeps eastward across southeast Wyoming and western Nebraska, with orographically driven showers falling across the Northern Laramie, Snowy and Sierra Madre Ranges.

Saturday...A windy and colder day is in tap in the decent thickness packing behind the Pacific origin cold front, with winds decreasing in the afternoon as pressure gradients slacken off. The next closed low aloft moves near the Four Corners by early evening, and with orographics combined with diffluence aloft and adequate low and mid level moisture, you can expect scattered afternoon showers from the Sierra Madre Range e

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: The upper low is forecast to lift through the forecast area Thursday night into Friday, focusing precipitation across northern Utah and southwest Wyoming.
SLC.text:
Early afternoon satellite imagery shows an upper low spinning off the CA coast near 130W, while a fetch of low-mid level southerly flow is beginning to pull tropical moisture from the Baja region northward. As this upstream low begins to move inland, this moisture will quickly spread northward into southern Utah by Wednesday morning, and into central Utah by afternoon, bringing the potential for heavy rainfall and flash flooding. This moisture will remain in place through Thursday, resulting in a relatively long-duration window of potentially heavy rainfall across central and southern Utah, where storm totals may locally exceed 5" in upslope-favored areas such as the Pine Valleys and areas near Brian Head. As such have gone ahead with a Flood Watch for much of southern and eastern Utah for Wednesday through Thursday evening.

As the area comes under the influence of the upstream low Wednesday, enhanced low and deep layer shear combined with low LCLs will support supercells capable of all severe weather hazards assuming sufficient instability is able to develop. This appears most likely to occur across southwest Utah in closer proximity to the upper dynamics. This threat will persist into Thursday and expand northward into central and perhaps northern Utah assuming sufficient instability.

The upper low is forecast to lift through the forecast area Thursday night into Friday, focusing precipitation across northern Utah and southwest Wyoming. As colder air spreads into the area, snow levels will fall to around 8500 feet with accumulating snow likely above 9000 feet. Snow accumulations of 2-6 inches above 9000 feet look likely, with the potential for higher totals depending on how the upper low evolves as it lifts through the region. A secondary trough digging into the region may keep precipitation going into the weekend, although confidence is fairly low at this time with respect to how the overall pattern evolves.

BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: Cool and wet conditions will continue as a broad low pressure system moves northeast on Friday.
BOI.text: Cool and wet conditions will continue as a broad low pressure system moves northeast on Friday. Breezy northwest winds with gusts ranging from 30-45 mph, widespread rain over southwest Idaho, and cool temperatures about 5-8 degrees below normal are anticipated during the day on Friday. Snow levels will lower by Friday afternoon, down to around 6000-7000 ft MSL. Higher elevation passes and ridgetops will likely only see a dusting of snow, with summits seeing close to an inch as the precipitation tapers off early Saturday. Drying conditions and near normal temperatures will return for the weekend thanks to a building ridge of high pressure over the West Coast. By late Sunday, long range forecast models begin to diverge. Some ensemble members favor a closed low pressure system moving onshore and bringing much cooler and wetter conditions by early next week, while other deterministic runs favor high pressure lingering over the Intermountain West through the middle of next week. Current forecast favors ridging and a slight warming and drying trend through Monday, with a slight chance of precipitation over the West Central Mountains.
